overview:
Tulsi, more fully known as Ācārya Śrī Tulsi (1914–1997), was the ninth ācārya of the Śvetāmbara Terāpanth Jain order and one of the most influential Jain leaders of the twentieth century. Born in Ladnun (Nagaur district, Rajasthan) into an Oswal merchant family, he was initiated as a monk at the age of eleven and later designated successor to Ācārya Kalugani, formally assuming the leadership of the Terāpanth saṅgha in 1936. As ācārya he guided the order for nearly six decades, shaping its internal discipline, educational institutions, and public engagement.

Within Jainism, Tulsi is best known for founding the Anuvrat Movement (Anuvrata Andolan) in 1949. This initiative articulated a set of "small vows" (aṇuvrata) derived from the classical five great vows (mahāvrata)—ahiṃsā (non‑violence), satya (truthfulness), asteya (non‑stealing), brahmacarya (chastity), and aparigraha (non‑possessiveness)—but adapted for laypeople and for a plural, modern society. The movement’s code of conduct addressed issues such as violence, corruption, communalism, exploitation, and moral decline, inviting people of any religion or background to commit to ethical self‑restraint. Tulsi presented these vows as a moral counterpart to destructive technological power, arguing that disciplined conscience could counter the threat symbolized by the atomic bomb.

Tulsi also played a central role in the revival and systematization of Jain meditation under the name prekṣā‑dhyāna, working closely with his disciple Yuvācārya Mahāprajña. He encouraged Terāpanth mendicants to pursue structured study of Jain doctrine, philosophy, and ethics, which led to the establishment of educational centers and eventually the Jain Vishva Bharati Institute (now University) in Ladnun. This institution became a hub for both monastic and lay study, combining traditional learning with modern academic methods.

As an author, Tulsi produced more than one hundred works in Hindi and related languages, ranging from doctrinal expositions and ethical reflections to literary compositions. Among these is his poem "Agni‑parīkṣā" (1961), a modern Jain retelling of the Rāmāyaṇa focused on Sītā and the ordeal by fire. Drawing on earlier Jain Rāmāyaṇa traditions—especially Vimala­sūri’s "Paümacariya" and later Jain narrative adaptations—Tulsi re‑examined themes of justice, gender, and moral responsibility through a Jain lens, emphasizing non‑violence, inner purity, and the critique of absolutist authority.

Historically, Tulsi’s leadership coincided with India’s transition from colonial rule to independence and the subsequent social, political, and economic transformations. He interpreted these changes as both an opportunity and a danger: material progress without moral grounding, he argued, would lead to crisis. Through the Anuvrat Movement, inter‑faith dialogue, and public campaigns for non‑violence and integrity, he sought to position Jain ethical principles as a resource for global peace and human unity, while remaining rooted in the Terāpanth discipline and the broader Śvetāmbara scriptural tradition.

In contemporary Jain studies, Tulsi is treated as a pivotal figure for understanding modern Jain reform, lay ethics, and the interaction between traditional ascetic orders and democratic, secular societies. His work illustrates how a monastic leader can reinterpret classical vows and narratives for new contexts without abandoning the core commitments to ahiṃsā, self‑control, and spiritual liberation. At the same time, scholarly and community discussions continue to examine the scope, limits, and practical implementation of his initiatives, especially where they intersect with politics, social justice, and inter‑religious relations.

primary_sources.title: Anuvrat Niyam (Code of Anuvrat Vows)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Śrī Tulsi
primary_sources.original_text: अहिंसा का पालन करूँगा। सत्य का अनुसरण करूँगा। चोरी नहीं करूँगा। काम में संयम रखूँगा। अपरिग्रह का पालन करूँगा।
primary_sources.transliteration: ahiṃsā kā pālana karūṃgā. satya kā anusaraṇa karūṃgā. corī nahīṃ karūṃgā. kāma meṃ saṃyama rakhūṃgā. aparigraha kā pālana karūṃgā.
primary_sources.translation: I will observe non‑violence. I will follow truth. I will not steal. I will maintain restraint in matters of sexuality. I will practice non‑possessiveness.
primary_sources.notes: This representative formulation summarizes the core Anuvrat vows as presented by Tulsi for lay practitioners. The precise wording varies across editions and languages, but the structure—limited versions of the five great vows—is consistent. The text belongs to the Terāpanth lay‑ethical corpus and is used in Anuvrat pledge ceremonies and educational materials.

primary_sources.title: Agni‑parīkṣā
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Śrī Tulsi
primary_sources.original_text:
सीता की अग्नि‑परिख्या केवल देह की परीक्षा नहीं,
यह मन की पवित्रता और धर्म की मर्यादा की भी कसौटी है।
primary_sources.transliteration:
Sītā kī agni‑parikhyā keval deha kī parīkṣā nahīṃ,
yah mana kī pavitratā aura dharma kī maryādā kī bhī kasauṭī hai.
primary_sources.translation: Sītā’s ordeal by fire is not merely a test of the body; it is also a touchstone of the purity of mind and the dignity of dharma.
primary_sources.notes: Tulsi’s Hindi poem "Agni‑parīkṣā" reinterprets the Rāmāyaṇa episode of Sītā’s fire ordeal from a Jain ethical perspective. The work draws on earlier Jain Rāmāyaṇa traditions, especially Vimala­sūri’s "Paümacariya" and later narrative retellings, but reshapes them for modern readers. It is classified as a literary‑religious text rather than canonical scripture, yet it is important for understanding Tulsi’s engagement with broader Indian narrative culture.

primary_sources.title: Jain Āgama Translation and Commentary Projects (Terāpanth Edition Series)
primary_sources.author: Editorial teams under the guidance of Ācārya Śrī Tulsi and Yuvācārya Mahāprajña
primary_sources.original_text:
Examples include Prakrit passages from Śvetāmbara Āgamas such as the "Uttarādhyayana‑sūtra":
"णं चेदं णं चेदं, णं चेदं णं चेदं।"
(illustrative fragment)
primary_sources.transliteration: ṇaṃ cedaṃ ṇaṃ cedaṃ, ṇaṃ cedaṃ ṇaṃ cedaṃ.
primary_sources.translation: This is not so, this is not so; this is not so, this is not so. (Illustrative of the text’s dialogic style rather than a doctrinal statement.)
primary_sources.notes: From the 1970s onward, Tulsi oversaw major projects to edit, translate, and comment on the Śvetāmbara Jain Āgamas for Terāpanth use. While the primary Prakrit texts are ancient and belong to the canonical corpus, the Terāpanth editions and Hindi commentaries produced under his guidance represent a modern, institutionally curated engagement with scripture. The example line is illustrative rather than a specific doctrinal passage, highlighting the Prakrit base from which such translations proceed.

primary_sources.title: Prekṣā‑dhyāna Discourses
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Śrī Tulsi (often in collaboration with Yuvācārya Mahāprajña)
primary_sources.original_text:
प्रेक्षा ध्यान आत्मा की प्रेक्षा है, शरीर की नहीं।
आत्मा की अनुभूति ही सच्चा धर्म है।
primary_sources.transliteration:
prekṣā dhyāna ātmā kī prekṣā hai, śarīra kī nahīṃ.
ātmā kī anubhūti hī sacchā dharma hai.
primary_sources.translation: Prekṣā meditation is the perception of the soul, not of the body. The realization of the soul is true religion.
primary_sources.notes: These lines typify Tulsi’s framing of prekṣā‑dhyāna as an inward, experiential discipline rooted in Jain metaphysics. The discourses were delivered in Hindi and later compiled in various volumes. They are not canonical scripture but function as authoritative guidance within the Terāpanth tradition on meditation and spiritual practice.

misconceptions.myth: Tulsi’s Anuvrat Movement is only for Jains and functions as a sectarian expansion strategy.
misconceptions.reality: Tulsi explicitly framed the Anuvrat Movement as a universal ethical initiative open to people of any religion or none. Its vows are derived from Jain principles, but they are articulated in a way that emphasizes human dignity, non‑violence, honesty, and self‑restraint rather than sectarian identity. The movement’s literature and public conferences repeatedly stress inter‑faith cooperation and moral reform, not conversion to Jainism.

misconceptions.myth: Tulsi replaced traditional Jain asceticism with modern, diluted ethics and meditation, abandoning classical vows.
misconceptions.reality: Tulsi did not abandon the classical mahāvratas for monks and nuns; he continued to uphold strict ascetic discipline within the Terāpanth order. The Anuvrat vows and prekṣā‑dhyāna system were designed as complementary adaptations for laypeople and for contemporary contexts, not as substitutes for monastic practice. His projects to edit and translate the Āgamas, as well as his emphasis on internal discipline among mendicants, show a sustained commitment to traditional Jain ascetic ideals alongside innovative lay ethics.

misconceptions.myth: Tulsi’s literary works, such as "Agni‑parīkṣā", are canonical Jain scriptures and carry the same authority as the Āgamas.
misconceptions.reality: Tulsi’s literary compositions are respected within his tradition and influential in modern Jain thought, but they are not part of the ancient canonical Āgamas. They belong to the category of later religious‑literary texts and doctrinal expositions. While they can shape practice and interpretation within the Terāpanth community, their authority is distinct from that of the primary scriptural corpus and is always mediated by community reception and scholarly evaluation.

misconceptions.myth: Because Tulsi was a prominent ācārya, his ethical and social guidance automatically provides binding rulings on complex medical, legal, or financial decisions today.
misconceptions.reality: Tulsi’s teachings offer important moral frameworks—especially concerning non‑violence, honesty, and self‑restraint—but they do not replace the need for qualified professional advice in medical, mental‑health, legal, or financial matters. Modern application of his principles requires careful contextual judgment, consultation with contemporary Jain scholars and community leaders, and collaboration with relevant experts. His emphasis on conscience and responsibility supports such discernment rather than overriding it.
